Google says Chrome cuts 7 billion unwanted Android notifications a day to fight abuse

Google says Chrome’s layered anti-abuse systems cut more than 7 billion unwanted Android notifications per day in Q1 2026 by automatically revoking risky or inactive site permissions, limiting abusive senders, and improving user controls.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Google says Chrome's anti-abuse systems reduced unwanted notifications on Android by more than 7 billion per day during the first quarter of 2026.
  • 02Google says notification abuse is increasingly used to distribute scams, malware, phishing attempts, and fraudulent payment requests.
  • 03Chrome can automatically revoke notification permissions from inactive websites and from sites that repeatedly trigger suspicious-notification warnings.
  • 04Google analyzes behavior across networks of related websites, including coordinated service-worker activity, to identify groups distributing malicious or deceptive notifications.
  • 05Sites classified as disruptive can be limited to 1,000 messages per minute, with excess requests returning an HTTP 429 error.

Google says Chrome’s anti-abuse systems reduced unwanted notifications on Android by more than 7 billion per day during the first quarter of 2026. The company said notification abuse is increasingly used to distribute scams, malware, phishing attempts, and fraudulent payment requests. Google described its approach as a layered “Swiss cheese” defense model designed to stop abuse at different stages if one layer fails.

Chrome can automatically remove notification permissions from inactive websites and from sites that repeatedly trigger suspicious-notification warnings. When this happens, Chrome can automatically unsubscribe the user from a site’s notifications, while still allowing users to review revoked permissions in Safety Hub and grant access again. Users can also unsubscribe from notifications directly from Android’s notifications panel.

Google said it analyzes behavior across networks of related websites, including coordinated service-worker activity, to identify groups distributing malicious or deceptive notifications. It also considers factors such as notification volume, time users spend on a site, permission-prompt frequency, and engagement. Sites classified as disruptive can be limited to 1,000 messages per minute, with excess requests returning an HTTP 429 error, and restrictions can become more aggressive for repeat offenders.

  • Chrome’s defenses do not rely only on whether a single website looks malicious; Google also evaluates networks of related sites and coordinated service-worker activity to find persistent bad actors.
  • Automatic permission revocation can unsubscribe users from a site’s notifications, but users can still review those revoked permissions in Safety Hub and grant access again.
  • Google uses behavioral signals such as notification volume, time spent on a site, prompt frequency, and engagement to decide when notification activity is disruptive.
  • Google says repeat offenders can face increasingly aggressive restrictions, and those restrictions are reset only after a period of non-disruptive behavior.

Google says Chrome reduced unwanted notifications on Android by more than 7 billion per day in early 2026. This matters because abusive notifications are being used to push scams, malicious software, phishing attempts, and fake payment requests to everyday users. Chrome can now automatically turn off notification permissions for inactive or suspicious websites, limit sites that send too many messages, and let users review or restore those choices if they want.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This reports a specific Google finding and product-defense update with broad relevance because Chrome on Android is widely used and abusive notifications are tied to scams, malware, phishing, and fraudulent payment requests. It is not an urgent active-exploitation or patch story, but it is useful for security professionals tracking browser abuse controls and user-protection mechanisms.

SHOULD · 84 research 12 Aug 2026 16:05 UTC · gpt-5.5

Plug and Pwn attack uses fake USB devices for Windows SYSTEM access

Researchers demonstrated “Plug and Pwn” attacks that abuse Windows Plug and Play to make fake USB devices trigger automatic vendor driver/software installs running as SYSTEM, enabling privilege escalation even with no logged-in user. Some variants can also be launched remotely through RDP USB redirection, and mitigations like disabling co-installers help but do not fully remove the attack surface.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Security researchers Alejandro Hernando and Borja Martínez disclosed “Plug and Pwn” attacks at DEF CON 34 that abuse Windows Plug and Play to install vulnerable or insecure vendor software as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM.
  • 02The researchers used FaceDancer with Cynthion and GreatFET hardware to emulate USB devices, causing Windows to recognize fake hardware and install associated vendor driver packages.
  • 03A zero-click physical demonstration impersonated Sierra Wireless and Sony FeliCa devices to change DNS settings, redirect unencrypted downloads, place a malicious file on the system, and open a reverse shell with SYSTEM privileges on a fully updated Windows 11 computer with nobody logged in.
  • 04The researchers also demonstrated “NoPlug & Pwn,” which uses RDP USB redirection and a custom Python RDP client to make a remote Windows host treat fake USB descriptors as a legitimate device and install vendor software as SYSTEM.
  • 05Setting the DisableCoInstallers registry value can disrupt some demonstrated attacks, including the Sony FeliCa and Intel RealSense RDP chains, but Hernando said it does not stop the broader attack class.

Security researchers Alejandro Hernando and Borja Martínez disclosed new “Plug and Pwn” attacks at DEF CON 34 that abuse Windows Plug and Play. The attacks can cause Windows to install signed vendor packages that contain exploitable components or weaknesses and run them as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. Some demonstrated chains require no user interaction or logged-in user, and one can be performed remotely over RDP without physical USB hardware connected to the target.

The researchers used FaceDancer with Cynthion and GreatFET hardware to emulate USB devices and make Windows identify them as specific hardware. In one zero-click physical demonstration, they impersonated Sierra Wireless and Sony FeliCa devices to change DNS settings, redirect unencrypted downloads, place a malicious file on the system, and later load it to open a reverse shell with SYSTEM privileges. They said this worked against a fully updated Windows 11 computer with nobody logged in and took about five minutes.

They also demonstrated “NoPlug & Pwn,” which abuses RDP USB redirection by sending fake USB descriptors through a Python RDP client. The remote Windows host treats the descriptors as a legitimate USB device and installs the matching driver and vendor software as SYSTEM, including an Intel RealSense camera package that can be abused through DLL hijacking. The article says setting the DisableCoInstallers registry value can break some demonstrated chains, but Hernando said it does not remove the broader attack surface and recommended pairing it with device installation restrictions or hardware-ID allow-lists and disabling Plug and Play device redirection where it is not needed.

  • Disabling co-installers is only a partial mitigation because Plug and Pwn can still use Plug and Play enumeration, Windows Update driver resolution, driver staging, INF processing, and INF-installed services.
  • RDP USB redirection expands the risk beyond physical access because a custom RDP client can send fake USB descriptors to a remote Windows host when that feature is enabled.
  • Composite USB device presentation is important to some attack chains because it causes Windows to load usbccgp.sys and enumerate interfaces separately, making Windows match vendor packages instead of inbox drivers.
  • The demonstrated chains rely on legitimate signed vendor packages and normal Windows device installation behavior, so the researchers said not all scenarios were reported as standalone vendor vulnerabilities.
  • For sensitive systems, Hernando recommended combining DisableCoInstallers with device installation restrictions or hardware-ID allow-lists and disabling Plug and Play device redirection on RDP and VDI hosts that do not need it.

Security researchers showed that Windows can be tricked by fake USB devices into automatically installing trusted-looking device software that gives the attacker the highest level of control on the computer. Some versions need only a small device plugged in, while another can work through a remote desktop connection if USB sharing is enabled, even without real USB hardware. This matters because fully updated Windows 11 computers, including ones with nobody logged in, can be affected, and the researchers say simple fixes reduce some risk but do not remove the broader problem.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a specific new research disclosure with broad relevance to Windows environments because it shows Plug and Play can be abused for SYSTEM-level privilege escalation using fake USB devices and, in some cases, RDP USB redirection. It is not described as active exploitation in the wild or an emergency patch event, but the zero-click and remote demonstrations make it important for security professionals to understand and mitigate.

"City-Forum" data-theft attacks target Salesforce, ServiceNow portals

A campaign dubbed City-Forum is stealing data from misconfigured Salesforce Experience Cloud and ServiceNow customer portals that expose records to unauthenticated guest users. The activity is ongoing and appears to come from a single long-running Contabo-hosted IP, with defenders urged to lock down guest access, public APIs, self-registration, and portal search sources.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Reco says an ongoing data theft campaign dubbed City-Forum is using custom tools to steal data exposed to anonymous users through Salesforce Experience Cloud and ServiceNow customer portals.
  • 02The attacks have been traced to the IP address 158.220.87.79, hosted by German VPS provider Contabo and associated with the city-forum.com domain since at least March 2025.
  • 03Reco says the campaign is not exploiting vulnerabilities in Salesforce or ServiceNow, but is abusing overly permissive guest-user sharing rules, permissions, or portal configurations.
  • 04On Salesforce, the attacker targets Aura endpoints and newer Lightning Web Runtime sites to enumerate and retrieve records exposed to guest accounts.
  • 05On ServiceNow, the attacker targets the POST /api/now/sp/search?sysparm_cancelable=true endpoint to search Service Portals that allow guest access to data.

An ongoing data theft campaign dubbed City-Forum is using custom tools to steal data exposed to anonymous users through Salesforce Experience Cloud and ServiceNow customer portals. SaaS security firm Reco traced the campaign to a single server that has targeted organizations worldwide, including telecommunications companies, banks and financial services firms, enterprise software vendors, security and data privacy companies, and public-sector portals. Reco says the attacks are ongoing and that activity continues to increase.

Reco says the attacks originate from the IP address 158.220.87.79, hosted by German VPS provider Contabo, and usually use the default Go-http-client/1.1 user agent when downloading data. The campaign is not exploiting a vulnerability in Salesforce or ServiceNow, but is abusing data that organizations have mistakenly exposed to unauthenticated guest users through overly permissive sharing rules, permissions, or portal configurations. The same infrastructure and fingerprint have been observed against both Salesforce and ServiceNow environments across multiple organizations.

On Salesforce, the attacker targets older Aura endpoints such as /aura or /s/sfsites/aura, invokes HostConfigController.getConfigData to enumerate objects, and uses SelectableListDataProviderController.getItems to retrieve records. The attacker also targets newer Lightning Web Runtime sites through GraphQL requests to /webruntime/api/services/data/{version}/graphql, and checks /SiteRegister and /CommunitiesSelfReg for self-registration. On ServiceNow, the attacker targets POST /api/now/sp/search?sysparm_cancelable=true, and Reco advises administrators to review guest access, public APIs, self-registration, and exposed portal search sources.

  • Reco observed the same fingerprint across both Salesforce and ServiceNow environments, suggesting defenders can look for the combination of IP address 158.220.87.79 and the default Go-http-client/1.1 user agent across multiple portal platforms.
  • The campaign includes Salesforce Lightning Web Runtime sites through GraphQL requests to the webruntime API, a technique Reco says it has not seen in public attack tools such as AuraInspector, S-RET, or CirrusGo.
  • Disabling the Experience Builder option that allows guest users to access public APIs can block several Salesforce API endpoints used for data enumeration and theft when guest API access is not required.
  • ServiceNow transaction logs do not record the POST body for the targeted portal search endpoint, so defenders may be able to see that automated searches occurred and how much data was returned but not the exact search terms used.

A data theft campaign called City-Forum is taking information from company customer portals built with Salesforce and ServiceNow when those portals have been set up to let public visitors see too much. The targets include telecom companies, banks, software vendors, security and privacy companies, and public-sector portals around the world. This matters because the attackers do not need to break into the systems if sensitive records are accidentally left open to anyone on the Internet, and the activity is still increasing.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a specific, ongoing data theft campaign targeting widely used Salesforce Experience Cloud and ServiceNow portals across multiple sectors worldwide. The article provides concrete indicators, targeted endpoints, and actionable configuration areas for defenders to review, making it highly relevant for security professionals.

Android malware combo takes out loans and relays victims' credit cards

Attackers are combining the SpyNote Android RAT with new WindRelay NFC malware to remotely control victims’ phones, take out loans, and relay live payment card data for fraudulent transactions. The attack relies heavily on phone-based social engineering, including convincing victims to sideload an app, grant permissions, tap their card to the phone, and enter their PIN.
KEY POINTS
  • 01A new Android NFC relay malware called WindRelay is being used with the SpyNote remote administration tool to steal card data and send it to attackers in real time.
  • 02In an incident investigated by Group-IB, a fraudster impersonated a bank employee, convinced the victim to sideload SpyNote disguised as a legitimate app, and obtained Accessibility Service permissions for remote access to the Android device.
  • 03After gaining remote access, the attacker installed WindRelay, used the victim’s banking app to take out a loan in the victim’s name, and instructed the victim to tap their payment card on the phone and enter their PIN.
  • 04Group-IB said the activity occurred during a 13-minute phone call, and the transactions were approved using the PIN provided by the victim.
  • 05Group-IB identified almost two dozen WindRelay samples submitted to VirusTotal between November 2025 and July 2026, with targeting appearing focused on Czechia, Slovakia, and Slovenia.

A new Android NFC relay malware called WindRelay is being used together with the SpyNote remote administration tool to steal card data and send it to attackers in real time. In an incident investigated by Group-IB, a fraudster impersonated a bank employee and convinced the victim to sideload SpyNote disguised as a legitimate app. The attacker also had the victim grant Accessibility Service permissions, giving remote access to the Android device.

After gaining access through SpyNote, the attacker installed WindRelay without further interaction from the victim and used the banking app to take out a loan in the victim’s name. The victim was then instructed to tap their payment card on the phone and enter their PIN. WindRelay turned the phone into a fraudulent contactless reader and relayed the live NFC exchange, including transaction-specific authentication data, to the attacker’s device for purchases at a genuine payment terminal.

Group-IB said the entire activity occurred during a 13-minute phone call, and transactions were approved using the PIN provided by the victim. The researchers said the combination may indicate a toolkit that provides both access to a victim’s device for banking transactions and a direct cash-out channel. Group-IB identified almost two dozen WindRelay samples submitted to VirusTotal between November 2025 and July 2026, with apparent targeting focused on Czechia, Slovakia, and Slovenia.

  • The combination of SpyNote and WindRelay gives attackers both remote access to a victim’s banking app and a direct way to cash out through relayed card transactions.
  • The attack did not require the victim to interact with WindRelay directly after SpyNote was installed, because the attacker used remote access to install WindRelay without further victim interaction.
  • The fraud succeeded without relying on modern malware features such as live screen sharing or VNC, showing that phone-based social engineering alone was enough to guide the victim through the theft.
  • Personalizing the malicious app label with the victim’s name was used to make the fake app appear more credible during the social engineering call.
  • A practical defensive step from the article is to hang up on urgent bank calls and call the official number from the organization’s website before taking any requested action.

The article describes criminals calling people while pretending to be bank employees, then convincing them to install a harmful Android app and tap their payment card on the phone. In one case, the criminals remotely used the victim’s phone to take out a loan in the victim’s name and used the card information to make purchases during a 13-minute call. Android users, especially in Czechia, Slovakia, and Slovenia, are affected, and the broader risk is that a phone call plus a fake app can lead quickly to real financial theft.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a specific in-the-wild Android banking fraud case involving named malware families, real-time NFC card relaying, and documented targeting in multiple European countries. It is broadly relevant to security professionals tracking mobile threats and social-engineering-enabled financial fraud, though it is not a critical patch or major breach.

Signal adds new security feature to thwart man-in-the-middle attacks

Signal has launched Automatic Key Verification, a key-transparency feature that uses independent auditors to help confirm contacts’ encryption keys and detect man-in-the-middle key swaps without manual safety-number checks. Users can enable it in privacy settings or continue relying on manual verification.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Signal introduced Automatic Key Verification, a new security feature designed to help users ensure their encrypted chats have not been intercepted.
  • 02The feature is part of a key transparency system that uses Cloudflare and Trail of Bits as trusted third-party independent auditors to verify the integrity of Signal conversations.
  • 03Signal says the system helps ensure that the association between a phone number or username and its public encryption key is globally consistent and transparent to all participants in Signal’s ecosystem.
  • 04Users can enable Automatic Key Verification in Signal by going to Settings, Privacy, Advanced, and toggling on Automatic Key Verification.
  • 05Users who do not want to rely on Signal or independent auditors can disable Automatic Key Verification and continue using manual safety number verification.

Signal has introduced Automatic Key Verification, a new security feature that gives users another way to ensure their encrypted chats have not been intercepted. The feature is part of a key transparency system that uses Cloudflare and Trail of Bits as trusted third-party independent auditors to verify the integrity of Signal conversations. Signal says the system provides the same assurance as manually verifying safety numbers, but without requiring an in-person meeting or a secondary communication channel.

The system is designed to ensure that the link between a phone number or username and its public encryption key is globally consistent and transparent across Signal’s ecosystem. Signal says this protects against scenarios where a key is swapped without the key owner’s knowledge, such as if a malicious party compromised Signal and associated a different key with a contact’s phone number. Users can enable Automatic Key Verification in Settings > Privacy > Advanced, or verify a contact by selecting “Verify Automatically” on the safety number verification screen.

Users who do not want to rely on Signal or independent auditors can disable Automatic Key Verification and continue using manual safety number verification. The article also notes that Signal recently added warning messages and in-app confirmations to help users evaluate external requests after attacks attributed to Russian state-sponsored hackers abused Signal’s Linked Device feature. Those attacks targeted high-profile users with bogus “Signal Support” alerts to gain access to accounts, chats, and contact lists.

  • Automatic Key Verification is meant to provide the same assurance as manual safety number checks while removing the need for an in-person meeting or a second communication channel.
  • Signal’s design uses both user-side checks and third-party auditors, which means key consistency is not verified only by Signal itself.
  • The feature specifically addresses a high-impact scenario in which a malicious party compromises Signal and silently associates a different encryption key with a user’s phone number or username.
  • Signal preserved a manual verification path for users who do not want to rely on Signal or the independent auditors.
  • Signal’s recent security changes follow reported Russian state-sponsored phishing campaigns that abused the Linked Device feature to access targets’ accounts, chats, and contact lists.

Signal added a new feature called Automatic Key Verification to help users confirm that the person they are messaging is really linked to the correct security key, without needing to meet in person or check through another app. This matters for Signal users because it can help reveal if someone secretly swapped a key to read or interfere with private chats. The feature also comes after warnings about attackers targeting Signal users with fake support messages to take over accounts and access chats and contacts.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a specific security feature launch in a widely used encrypted messaging app, with broad relevance for professionals tracking secure communications and man-in-the-middle protections. It is not an urgent incident or critical patch, but it is actionable because users can enable Automatic Key Verification and understand how Signal is changing key verification.

The Threat Hiding in Your Hiring Process: How Fake Remote Workers Get In

Fake remote workers, including North Korean IT operatives, can bypass hiring checks by using forged identities, proxies, and remote access to gain legitimate company access. The key takeaway is that organizations should verify the live person receiving and using access, not just the documents and résumé submitted during hiring.
KEY POINTS
  • 01The US Department of State warned in July that North Korean IT workers impersonate nationals of other countries to obtain work and send their salaries back to parent agencies in North Korea.
  • 02The FBI has warned that fraudulent workers may use their access to copy source-code repositories, exfiltrate proprietary information, support other cybercriminal activity, and attempt extortion after being discovered or dismissed.
  • 03Fake remote-worker operations can use forged identity documents, fabricated résumés, proxy interviewees, facilitator addresses, laptop farms, and third-party payment accounts to satisfy different hiring and onboarding controls.
  • 04Warning signs of a fake remote worker include frequent changes to registered information, payment-account name mismatches, multiple accounts using the same ID, unusual IP address patterns, and unusually high hours logged in.
  • 05Specops Software says organizations can strengthen onboarding by combining government-issued identity-document scanning with biometric liveness detection before access begins or service-desk agents make account changes.

The article describes how fake remote workers exploit hiring and onboarding processes to gain legitimate access to company systems. It cites a July US Department of State alert warning that North Korean IT workers impersonate nationals of other countries to obtain work and send salaries back to parent agencies in North Korea. It also cites an FBI warning that fraudulent workers may copy source-code repositories, exfiltrate proprietary information, support other cybercriminal activity, and attempt extortion after being discovered or dismissed.

The article emphasizes that traditional employment checks do not necessarily prove who is actually using a company laptop or account. A stolen or proxy-supplied document, fabricated résumé, proxy interviewee, facilitator address, laptop farm, and third-party payment account can each satisfy separate controls while leaving the account under someone else’s control. Warning signs include frequent changes to registered information, mismatched payment-account names, multiple accounts using the same ID, suspicious IP address patterns, and unusually high hours logged in.

The sponsored article promotes Specops Secure Onboarding as a way to add government-issued identity-document scanning and biometric liveness detection to onboarding. It says document checks can help confirm that an identity document is genuine, while biometric checks compare the person completing onboarding with the document photo. More than 737 browser extensions on the Chrome Web Store impersonated well-known VPN and proxy services while routing users’ traffic through SOCKS5 proxies operated by a single provider. The extensions impersonated brands including Proton VPN, NordVPN, Surfshark, ExpressVPN, and Cloudflare’s 1.1.1.1 DNS resolver. Socket researchers said the campaign used 40 publisher accounts and a shared analytics account.

The extensions were downloaded nearly 75,000 times, mainly by Russian users looking for tools to bypass blocked services in the country. Socket said that with all browser traffic forced through the relay, the operator’s server could read every destination, every TLS SNI value, the victim’s source IP, and any request body sent over plain HTTP. Based on strings found in the extensions, the campaign appears to have been an attempt to funnel customers to a subscription-based VPN service in Russia.

Socket identified several behaviors, including 520 extensions routing all browser traffic through SOCKS5 proxies on port 1082 and 104 extensions resolving proxy hostnames through Cloudflare or Google DNS-over-HTTPS. Some extensions advertised nonexistent premium servers in Japan, Singapore, Canada, Australia, and Turkey for subscription fraud. Google removed more than 200 related extensions, but Socket said over 500 were still available and recommended that users check for the listed extension IDs, remove any matches, and confirm Chrome’s proxy configuration is back to normal.

  • The campaign’s scale was obscured by fragmentation across 40 publisher accounts, but Socket linked the extensions through shared infrastructure, including a shared analytics account.
  • Even though the extensions used a proxy mechanism similar to legitimate services, Socket identified deception indicators such as brand impersonation, nonexistent premium locations, misleading reviewer disclosures, and remote configuration added after approval.
  • Some extensions used Cloudflare or Google DNS-over-HTTPS to resolve proxy hostnames, which Socket said helped protect the operator’s domain from scrutiny.
  • Because all browser traffic was forced through the relay, the operator could observe every destination, TLS SNI value, victim source IP, and any request body sent over plain HTTP.
  • The campaign appears to have targeted demand from Russian users seeking ways around blocked services, while strings in the extensions suggested an attempt to funnel customers to a subscription-based VPN service in Russia.

Researchers found more than 737 Chrome add-ons pretending to be well-known VPN and proxy services, including Proton VPN, NordVPN, Surfshark, ExpressVPN, and Cloudflare’s 1.1.1.1. These add-ons were downloaded nearly 75,000 times, mostly by Russian users trying to reach blocked services, and they sent people’s browser traffic through servers controlled by one provider. This matters because whoever ran those servers could see where users were going online, their internet address, and any unencrypted information they sent. Google removed more than 200 of the add-ons, but researchers said over 500 were still available, so affected users should remove them and check that Chrome’s traffic settings are back to normal.

The article describes a legacy Microsoft Entra ID WS-Trust autologon endpoint used by Entra Seamless SSO that can be reached directly from the internet with username and password requests. In testing, this path allowed password spraying without triggering the expected Smart Lockout response and without failed attempts appearing in standard Entra ID sign-in logs. The endpoint also returned AADSTS error codes that could distinguish wrong passwords from valid passwords blocked later by MFA or Conditional Access.

The author says this makes the endpoint a quieter and more informative password spray path than normal sign-in flows. Responses such as AADSTS50055, AADSTS50076, and AADSTS53003 indicated that a password was accepted before another control stopped the flow, which can confirm valid credentials even for MFA-protected accounts. The article notes that confirmed passwords can still support follow-on techniques such as adversary-in-the-middle phishing, device code flow abuse, session theft workflows, primary refresh token theft, helpdesk pretexting, and password reuse attacks.

The article recommends disabling the usernamemixed endpoint at the tenant level, blocking legacy authentication through Conditional Access, monitoring the Unified Audit Log for requests to autologon.microsoftazuread-sso.com, and moving toward passwordless authentication. It says the main reason to keep the endpoint enabled is support for Office 2013 clients older than the May 2015 update. The research builds on earlier work by Dr. Nestori Syynimaa, Secureworks Counter Threat Unit, and tools such as AADInternals and MSOLSpray, while focusing on current behavior around Smart Lockout, logging, and response leakage.

  • The article says the only reason to keep the usernamemixed endpoint enabled is support for Office 2013 clients older than the May 2015 update, making full disablement a practical one-policy fix for most tenants.
  • The endpoint is especially problematic because it combines several weaknesses at once: internet reachability, missing standard sign-in log visibility, unexpected Smart Lockout behavior, and responses detailed enough to distinguish wrong passwords from valid passwords blocked later.
  • Blocking legacy authentication through Conditional Access is described as the highest-leverage mitigation because Microsoft’s standard policy template covers WS-Trust as well as ROPC, ActiveSync, and other legacy authentication paths.
  • The article frames the issue as more than a logging gap, because the same legacy path that reduces defender visibility also changes the outcome of password spraying by making each failed-looking attempt more informative to the attacker.

The article explains that an older Microsoft sign-in path for Entra ID can let attackers try many passwords against Microsoft 365 accounts without triggering the usual lockout protection or showing up in the normal sign-in records. It can also tell attackers when they guessed the right password, even if another protection like a second login check or access rule stops them from getting in. This affects organizations that still have this older sign-in method enabled, especially if they use Microsoft 365 and Entra ID. The real-world risk is that attackers can quietly find working passwords and use them for later scams, account theft attempts, or attacks against other systems.

The UK’s ACRO Criminal Records Office was reprimanded after three intrusions went undetected for nearly two years due to unpatched Kentico vulnerabilities, ignored antivirus alerts, and unclear security responsibilities. Attackers staged sensitive data on nearly 11,000 people for possible theft, though ACRO could not confirm exfiltration because of insufficient logs.
KEY POINTS
  • 01The Information Commissioner’s Office reprimanded ACRO Criminal Records Office after three intrusions between July 2021 and June 2023 exposed personal data belonging to thousands of people, including victims of domestic violence.
  • 02All three attacks exploited ACRO’s public-facing customer portal, which used the Kentico content management system and had not received available security fixes since running the same version from September 2019.
  • 03Trend Micro security alerts during the attack period, including four detections of attempts to install the Mimikatz credential-harvesting tool, went unread or unhandled because ACRO could not identify a process or responsible roles for reviewing them.
  • 04The most serious incident involved an attacker maintaining persistent access to ACRO’s website and content management system for about seven months and staging sensitive data of just under 11,000 people for exfiltration in February 2023.
  • 05ACRO notified more than 84,000 people as a precaution in April 2023, and the ICO said network segmentation prevented the attacker from moving beyond the compromised web environment into the core policing system.

Britain’s ACRO Criminal Records Office has been reprimanded by the Information Commissioner’s Office after three intrusions went undetected over nearly two years. The breaches exposed personal data belonging to thousands of people, including victims of domestic violence. ACRO is a national policing unit that handles sensitive data stored on the Police National Computer.

The ICO said all three attacks exploited ACRO’s public-facing customer portal, which was built on the Kentico content management system. The system had been running the same version since September 2019 despite multiple known and publicly documented vulnerabilities, and available security fixes had not been applied. ACRO, its managed service provider, and its web development supplier did not know who was responsible for monitoring and applying those patches.

The most serious incident involved an attacker maintaining access to ACRO’s website and content management system for about seven months and staging sensitive data of just under 11,000 people for exfiltration. ACRO could not confirm whether that data was actually exfiltrated because it had not retained sufficient logs. The ICO said network segmentation prevented the attacker from moving beyond the compromised web environment into the core policing system, and ACRO has since decommissioned the compromised infrastructure and implemented a new security information and event management system.

  • ACRO’s failures were not limited to missing patches or alerts; the ICO found that ACRO, its managed service provider, and its web development supplier did not know who was responsible for monitoring and applying Kentico security fixes.
  • The lack of sufficient logging meant ACRO could not confirm whether the staged data of just under 11,000 people was actually exfiltrated, limiting its ability to determine the true impact of the incident.
  • Security tooling was present and generated relevant warnings, including detections tied to Mimikatz, but those warnings did not reduce the damage because ACRO could not establish a business process for reviewing or escalating them.
  • The ICO issued only a reprimand with no financial penalty, citing network segmentation that prevented movement from the compromised web environment into the core policing system as a mitigating factor.

Britain’s ACRO Criminal Records Office was officially reprimanded after hackers broke into its public website area three times over nearly two years without being noticed. The personal information of thousands of people may have been exposed, including domestic violence victims, and more than 84,000 people who had applied to the database were warned as a precaution. The case matters because basic missed protections, such as not fixing known website problems and not reading warning messages, allowed attackers to stay inside systems holding highly sensitive police-related data.

CISA ordered federal agencies to patch Windows vulnerability CVE-2026-68820 by August 25 after CISA and Microsoft confirmed it is being exploited. The bug affects Winsock, which the article describes as a tool that acts as a bridge allowing web browsers to connect to the internet. Microsoft said it was the only vulnerability in its Patch Tuesday release confirmed to be used in real-world attacks.

The vulnerability is tied to a North Korean hacking campaign targeting people applying for jobs in the defense and aerospace industry. Check Point said it disclosed the bug to Microsoft after finding it during research into the latest wave of Operation “Dream Job,” a long-running campaign by North Korean hackers to exploit the job application process. Lazarus Group hackers allegedly impersonated recruiters for Lockheed Martin and Enveil, contacted people on LinkedIn and other sites, and sent malicious PDF files that enabled a backdoor for long-term remote access.

Check Point researchers said the malware first collects information about the infected device before deploying an exploit for CVE-2026-68820. The flaw allows an attacker who already placed malware on a machine to escalate from limited access to complete control normally reserved for the operating system itself. Researchers found targets across defense-related sectors including surveillance sensors, drones, and robotics in France, Germany, Brazil, and India.

  • The article says there is no workaround for CVE-2026-68820 and a restart is required, making patch deployment the only stated remediation path for affected Windows endpoints.
  • Jason Kikta noted that exploitation requires an attacker to first gain a low-privileged foothold through phishing, so blocking or detecting the initial fake recruiting activity is part of reducing exposure to the Windows flaw.
  • Check Point said Lazarus made the campaign harder to detect by using trusted infrastructure, real vendor branding, and already-compromised organizations rather than relying only on obviously suspicious links.
  • Check Point initially believed the issue was related to a vulnerability fixed last year, but testing showed it was a new bug, highlighting that similar-looking exploit activity may still involve a distinct vulnerability.

U.S. federal agencies have been told to fix a Windows problem by August 25 because North Korean hackers are already using it in attacks. The campaign targets people applying for jobs in defense and aerospace by posing as recruiters and sending harmful PDF files that can give the hackers long-term control over a person’s computer. This matters because the targets include sectors tied to surveillance sensors, drones and robotics in several countries, and the fake job messages can look very convincing because they use trusted names and real-looking websites.

Malicious LiteLLM Releases Tied to Trivy Hack May Have Exposed 2,100+ Organizations

Two malicious LiteLLM versions briefly published to PyPI in March may have exposed secrets from over 2,500 organizations, with attackers stealing cloud keys, CI/CD credentials, SSH keys, Kubernetes tokens, and other sensitive data. Organizations that installed LiteLLM 1.82.7 or 1.82.8 during the exposure window should rotate all accessible secrets immediately rather than wait for proof of misuse.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Two malicious LiteLLM releases, versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8, were live on PyPI for about 40 minutes on March 24 and contained code capable of stealing cloud keys, SSH keys, Kubernetes tokens, database passwords, and other secrets.
  • 02CloudSEK said a dataset built from roughly 434,000 files captured by the attackers maps potential exposure to more than 2,500 organizations, but the article states these totals are not a confirmed victim count.
  • 03The compromised packages sent stolen data to models.litellm[.]cloud, an attacker-controlled domain unrelated to the LiteLLM project.
  • 04The FBI warned that actors affiliated with the TeamPCP campaign are likely to use credentials stolen during the incident long after the initial compromise and advised organizations to rotate CI/CD secrets, publishing tokens, and cloud credentials.
  • 05Organizations assessing exposure are advised to check for LiteLLM 1.82.7 or 1.82.8 installations during the March 24 audit window, rotate accessible secrets, and search GitHub organizations for repositories named tpcp-docs or docs-tpcp.

Two malicious LiteLLM releases, versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8, were published on PyPI in March and carried code capable of stealing cloud keys, SSH keys, Kubernetes tokens, database passwords, and other secrets. LiteLLM said the versions were live on March 24 from 10:39 UTC for about 40 minutes before PyPI quarantined them, but it advises treating any install that day up to 16:00 UTC as suspect. CloudSEK said a dataset built from roughly 434,000 files captured by the attackers maps potential exposure to more than 2,500 organizations, though the article states this is not a confirmed victim count.

The compromised packages were designed to collect secrets and send stolen data to models.litellm[.]cloud, an attacker-controlled domain unrelated to the LiteLLM project. Version 1.82.8 included a litellm_init.pth file that Python processes at interpreter startup, meaning it ran whenever a Python process started in that environment even if LiteLLM was not imported. The article notes that an unpinned transitive dependency, including one pulled in by an agent framework or orchestration tool, could have delivered the compromised package without a team knowingly choosing LiteLLM.

The incident is tied to the wider TeamPCP supply-chain campaign linked to Aqua Security’s Trivy scanner, and Google tracks TeamPCP as UNC6780. The FBI warned that affiliated actors are likely to weaponize credentials stolen during the campaign long after the initial compromise and advised organizations to rotate CI/CD secrets, publishing tokens, and cloud credentials. Organizations assessing exposure are told to check for LiteLLM 1.82.7 or 1.82.8 installations during the March 24 audit window, rotate any secrets those systems could access, and search GitHub organizations for related campaign indicators.

  • Teams cannot limit their review to systems that intentionally used LiteLLM, because the article says an unpinned transitive dependency from an agent framework or orchestration tool could have installed the compromised package without anyone deliberately choosing it.
  • LiteLLM 1.82.8 was especially risky because its litellm_init.pth file ran when any Python process started in the environment, even if LiteLLM was never imported by an application.
  • CloudSEK’s public exposure dataset should be treated as a triage aid rather than a definitive victim list, because the article says it is based on stolen files and log data and does not prove that any stolen credentials were used.
  • Organizations searching GitHub for FBI-listed indicators may miss evidence if they only look for exact repository names, because Aqua’s advisory says the malware used a tpcp-docs- prefix and uploaded stolen data as release assets tagged data-<timestamp>.
  • The article frames credential rotation as urgent because long-lived secrets copied during the short exposure window can remain usable unless they have since been rotated or revoked.

Two harmful versions of LiteLLM, a tool used to connect apps to different AI services, were briefly available for download in March and were built to steal passwords, keys, and other secret access information from computers that installed them. CloudSEK says stolen files from the campaign point to possible exposure at more than 2,500 organizations, including major companies, though that does not prove the stolen access was later used. This matters because a copied password or key can keep working long after the original incident unless it is changed, so affected organizations are being told to replace any secrets those systems could reach.

ShieldBreak Zero-Day PoC Claims Microsoft Defender Patch Bypass With SYSTEM Access

A researcher released a PoC for ShieldBreak, a claimed Microsoft Defender zero-day that bypasses Microsoft’s patch for the earlier RoguePlanet flaw and can achieve SYSTEM-level privileges on current Windows versions. Microsoft has been contacted, while related Windows privilege-escalation flaws were addressed in the latest Patch Tuesday updates.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Security researcher Chaotic Eclipse released a proof-of-concept for ShieldBreak, a Microsoft Defender for Windows zero-day described as a patch bypass for CVE-2026-50656, also known as RoguePlanet.
  • 02RoguePlanet is a race condition that Microsoft described as a privilege escalation issue in the Microsoft Malware Protection Engine and that could allow an attacker to spawn a shell with SYSTEM-level privileges.
  • 03Chaotic Eclipse claimed the ShieldBreak proof-of-concept had a 100% success rate on the latest Windows 11 25H2 Canary channel and Windows Server 2025, and said Windows 10 and related server editions are also vulnerable but not currently supported by the PoC.
  • 04Microsoft’s August 2026 updates addressed 421 security flaws, including CVE-2026-62832, a Windows User Profile Service privilege escalation vulnerability disclosed by Chaotic Eclipse as LegacyHive.
  • 05Microsoft also patched CVE-2026-68820, an actively exploited Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock zero-day that grants SYSTEM privileges, and CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog with a required federal remediation date of August 25, 2026.

Security researcher Chaotic Eclipse, also known as INFINITE NIGHTMARE, MSNightmare, and Nightmare-Eclipse, released a proof-of-concept for a new Microsoft zero-day called ShieldBreak. The issue is rooted in Microsoft Defender for Windows and is described as a patch bypass for CVE-2026-50656, also known as RoguePlanet. RoguePlanet was previously described as a race condition that could allow an attacker to spawn a shell with SYSTEM-level privileges and run arbitrary code or perform unauthorized actions.

Microsoft patched RoguePlanet almost a month after its June 2026 disclosure, describing it as a privilege escalation issue in the Microsoft Malware Protection Engine, mpengine.dll. Chaotic Eclipse later said Microsoft’s defense-in-depth updates could cause Defender to leak 8 bytes of data in certain scenarios on Windows 11 25H2 and Windows Server 2025. The researcher now claims ShieldBreak is a full patch bypass, saying the proof-of-concept was tested on the latest Windows 11 25H2 Canary channel and Windows Server 2025 with a 100% success rate, while Windows 10 and related server editions are also described as vulnerable but not currently supported by the PoC.

The article also notes that Microsoft shipped patches for 421 security flaws, including 236 in Windows. These fixes include CVE-2026-62832, a Windows User Profile Service privilege escalation issue disclosed by Chaotic Eclipse as LegacyHive, as well as CVE-2026-68820, an actively exploited Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock zero-day that grants SYSTEM privileges. CISA added CVE-2026-68820 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and required federal agencies to apply fixes by August 25, 2026.

  • Microsoft’s prior fix for RoguePlanet is being challenged on two fronts: the researcher first reported an 8-byte data leak after the defense-in-depth updates, and now claims ShieldBreak is a full patch bypass.
  • The ShieldBreak PoC was claimed to work even on the latest Windows 11 25H2 Canary channel, indicating the researcher says pre-release builds with the newest changes are still affected.
  • Windows 10 and related server editions are described as vulnerable to ShieldBreak even though the released PoC does not currently support them, so lack of PoC support is not presented as lack of exposure.
  • The same researcher is tied to multiple recent Windows privilege escalation disclosures in the article, including RoguePlanet, ShieldBreak, and LegacyHive.
  • CISA’s action applies to CVE-2026-68820, not ShieldBreak, because the article says CVE-2026-68820 is actively exploited while Microsoft had not yet provided a response on ShieldBreak.

A security researcher released a public demonstration of a new problem in Microsoft Defender for Windows, saying Microsoft’s earlier fix for a related flaw did not fully solve it. The researcher says it can let someone who already has access to a Windows computer gain the highest level of control on Windows 11 25H2 and Windows Server 2025, and that Windows 10 is also vulnerable even though the demo does not support it yet. This matters because that level of control could let an attacker run their own programs or take actions they should not be allowed to take, while Microsoft is also fixing hundreds of other Windows security issues, including one already being used in real attacks.

SAP Commerce Cloud Flaw Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Arbitrary Code

SAP patched a critical SAP Commerce Cloud flaw (CVE-2026-58231) that could let unauthenticated attackers execute arbitrary code via insufficient authorization checks and input validation. Customers should update and redeploy fixed Commerce Cloud releases, or temporarily restrict access to the vulnerable endpoint with IP filtering.
KEY POINTS
  • 01SAP released patches for CVE-2026-58231, a maximum-severity flaw in SAP Commerce Cloud Data Hub Adapter rated 10.0 on the CVSS scale.
  • 02CVE-2026-58231 allows an unauthenticated attacker to abuse a default authentication client and submit specially crafted input to functions lacking sufficient validation, potentially enabling arbitrary code execution.
  • 03Onapsis urged customers to patch to a fixed SAP Commerce Cloud release and redeploy the updated version, with IP Filter Set restrictions suggested as a temporary workaround.
  • 04SAP’s August 2026 update also addressed critical flaws CVE-2026-44772, CVE-2026-34265, and CVE-2026-44758 affecting Manufacturing Integration and Intelligence, Application Server ABAP for SAP NetWeaver, and ABAP Platform.
  • 05Onapsis said SAP’s patch for CVE-2026-44758 removes a vulnerable servlet component, while the patch for CVE-2026-44772 requires maintaining the new 'Secure Transformer' system property with allowed hosts for XSL files.

SAP released patches for a maximum-severity security flaw in SAP Commerce Cloud Data Hub Adapter that could allow arbitrary code execution. The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-58231 and has a CVSS score of 10.0. It is described as involving insufficient authorization checks and input validation.

According to the CVE description, SAP Commerce Cloud allows an unauthenticated attacker to abuse a default authentication client and submit specially crafted input to certain functions that lack sufficient validation. Successful exploitation could compromise internal components and have a high impact on the application’s confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Onapsis urged customers to patch to a fixed Commerce Cloud release and redeploy the updated SAP Commerce Cloud version.

SAP’s August 2026 update also addressed three other critical vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-44772, CVE-2026-34265, and CVE-2026-44758. These affect Manufacturing Integration and Intelligence, Application Server ABAP for SAP NetWeaver, and ABAP Platform. Onapsis said temporary exposure to the Commerce Cloud flaw can be reduced by configuring an IP Filter Set, and it also described post-patch requirements for CVE-2026-44772 involving the new “Secure Transformer” system property and allowed hosts for XSL files.

  • For CVE-2026-58231, applying the fix is not just a patching step; Onapsis says customers must patch to a fixed SAP Commerce Cloud release and then redeploy the updated version.
  • Organizations that cannot immediately fix CVE-2026-58231 can reduce exposure by using an IP Filter Set to restrict access to the vulnerable endpoint.
  • SAP’s fix for CVE-2026-44758 removes the vulnerable servlet component entirely, indicating the remediation is a component removal rather than only input filtering or configuration hardening.
  • After patching CVE-2026-44772, customers must configure the new 'Secure Transformer' system property with allowed hosts for XSL files, or the post-patch control described by Onapsis is not in place.

SAP released fixes for a very serious problem in SAP Commerce Cloud, specifically its Data Hub Adapter, that could let someone with no login run their own code inside the system by abusing a default access method and sending specially crafted data. Organizations using the affected Commerce Cloud version are the ones who need to update and redeploy it, or temporarily limit who can reach the vulnerable part of the system. This matters because a successful attacker could take over internal parts of the application and harm the privacy, accuracy, and availability of the service.

Adobe Patches Three CVSS 10.0 ColdFusion and Campaign Classic Flaws

Adobe released urgent patches for critical ColdFusion, Commerce, and Campaign Classic vulnerabilities, including three CVSS 10.0 flaws that could allow arbitrary code execution. Administrators should apply the updates quickly, especially for ColdFusion and on-prem or hybrid Campaign Classic deployments.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Adobe shipped updates for critical vulnerabilities affecting ColdFusion, Commerce, and Campaign Classic that could lead to arbitrary code execution or privilege escalation.
  • 02The most severe issues include CVE-2026-48362 in ColdFusion and CVE-2026-71398 and CVE-2026-27302 in Campaign Classic, each rated CVSS 10.0.
  • 03ColdFusion fixes are included in versions 2025.0.12 and 2023.0.23, while Campaign Classic fixes are included in ACC v7 7.4.4 build 9400.

Adobe shipped updates to address multiple critical security vulnerabilities affecting ColdFusion, Commerce, and Campaign Classic. The flaws could allow arbitrary code execution, privilege escalation, or application denial-of-service if successfully exploited. The most severe issues include three CVSS 10.0 vulnerabilities across ColdFusion and Campaign Classic.

ColdFusion fixes are included in versions 2025.0.12 and 2023.0.23, while Campaign Classic fixes are included in ACC v7 7.4.4 build 9400. The listed issues include operating system command injection, eval injection, incorrect authorization, and SQL injection vulnerabilities. Adobe assigned the ColdFusion and Campaign Classic updates a Priority 1 rating, meaning they are considered at higher risk of being targeted by malicious cyber attacks.

The Campaign Classic updates apply only to fully on-premise deployments and to the on-premise components of hybrid deployments. Adobe-hosted instances have already been remediated and require no customer action. 737 Chrome VPN Extensions Caught Routing Traffic Through Proxies. Check If You Have One

Researchers found 737 Chrome VPN/proxy extensions, many impersonating major VPN brands, that routed users’ browser traffic through SOCKS5 proxies controlled by a single operator, exposing browsing destinations and some unencrypted data. Users should check for and remove suspicious or brand-impersonating Chrome VPN extensions.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Researchers found 737 free VPN and proxy Chrome extensions that mainly targeted Russian-speaking users seeking access to blocked services and routed browser traffic through proxy infrastructure.
  • 02The extensions were published across at least 40 Chrome Web Store developer accounts and accumulated 75,486 installs.
  • 03Socket reported that 274 of the extensions impersonated 66 established VPN and privacy brands, including Proton VPN, NordVPN, Surfshark, AdGuard VPN, Browsec, ExpressVPN, CyberGhost, Windscribe, TunnelBear, Cloudflare’s 1.1.1.1, and Google’s Outline.
  • 04Most of the extensions set Chrome’s proxy settings to a fixed SOCKS5 server on port 1082, allowing the operator to observe browser destinations, source IP addresses, TLS SNI values, and any request body sent over plain HTTP.

A set of 737 free VPN and proxy Chrome extensions was found to mainly target Russian-speaking users seeking access to blocked services. The extensions were published across at least 40 Chrome Web Store developer accounts and had 75,486 installs. Socket reported that 274 of them impersonated 66 established VPN and privacy brands, including Proton VPN, NordVPN, Surfshark, AdGuard VPN, ExpressVPN, Cloudflare’s 1.1.1.1, and Google’s Outline.

The extensions routed users’ browser sessions through SOCKS5 proxies, with 520 of 522 in the bulk corpus using the same SOCKS5 infrastructure. Most configured Chrome’s proxy settings to a fixed SOCKS5 server on port 1082, putting the operator in a position to observe browser destinations, source IP addresses, TLS SNI values, and any request body sent over plain HTTP. Each proxy-configuring extension used a bypass list limited to loopback addresses, so other browser requests were funneled through the relay once the user connected.

The article says 221 of the add-ons have been removed from the Chrome Web Store, while 516 remained active. Red flags included non-existent paid tiers, fake interfaces, DNS-over-HTTPS blocklist evasion, internal instructions in Russian, comments indicating attempts to evade Chrome Web Store policies, and false statements to reviewers. The article also describes Netskope Threat Labs’ finding that the “AI Sidebar with Deepseek, ChatGPT, Claude, and more.” extension returned with a monetization payload that opens an affiliate link whenever the extension updates or uninstalls.

  • The main warning sign was not VPN-like behavior itself, since the article says the functionality can resemble a legitimate VPN or proxy service, but the combination of brand impersonation, undisclosed proxy settings, fake premium servers, and false Chrome Web Store review statements.
  • Many extensions used a bypass list limited only to loopback addresses, meaning nearly every normal browser request would be sent through the proxy once the user connected to the supposed VPN service.
  • The extensions’ own package contents exposed operational clues, including a Russian taxpayer number, leaked Windows build paths, an internal Russian-language manual, and comments suggesting deliberate attempts to evade Chrome Web Store policies.
  • Chrome Web Store approval did not guarantee that an extension would remain benign, because the article describes extensions adding a remote-configuration layer or substituting code after approval.
  • The “AI Sidebar with Deepseek, ChatGPT, Claude, and more.” case shows that even an extension that removes earlier data-theft behavior can later return with a different unwanted payload through an update.

Researchers found 737 free Chrome add-ons pretending to be VPN or proxy tools, including many that copied the names of well-known privacy brands, and most of them sent users’ web browsing through servers controlled by the same operator. The add-ons mainly targeted Russian-speaking people trying to reach blocked services, and about 75,486 installations were counted. This matters because when someone used one of these add-ons, the operator could see what sites the browser was connecting to, the user’s internet address, and any information sent without encryption.

Enterprise Defenses Recovered at the Edge and Collapsed Inside

Picus Labs’ Blue Report 2026 finds enterprise defenses are improving at the perimeter but remain weak after attackers get inside, especially against quiet reconnaissance and credential-theft activity. The key gap is that organizations log more activity than before but rarely turn it into alerts or behavior-based prevention.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Picus Labs’ Blue Report 2026 measured more than 338 million real attack simulations across client production environments in the first half of 2026 and found average prevention effectiveness rose from 62% to 69%.
  • 02The report found that post-compromise prevention was only 37%, meaning defenses stopped barely one in three attacks once an adversary was already operating inside the network as an authenticated user.
  • 03Inside networks, noisy actions such as lateral movement through service execution and UAC-bypass privilege escalation were blocked around 90% and 85% of the time, while reconnaissance was stopped only 10% of the time.
  • 04The report found that credential theft using the classic LSASS memory-dumping path was blocked almost every time, but pulling credentials from other memory locations or the registry was almost never blocked.
  • 05Logging reached a four-year high of 58%, but the alert score stayed at 14%, meaning fewer than one in seven simulated attacks produced an alert.

Picus Labs’ Blue Report 2026 measured more than 338 million real attack simulations across client production environments in the first half of 2026. The report found that average prevention effectiveness rose from 62% to 69%, matching its 2024 peak, and logging reached a four-year high of 58%. The article says this recovery is real, but it is happening mostly at the perimeter.

The report found a major weakness after the perimeter is crossed, with a Post-Compromise Prevention Rate of only 37%. Inside networks, noisy actions such as lateral movement through service execution were stopped around 90% of the time, and UAC-bypass privilege escalation was blocked around 85% of the time. Quiet actions were far less likely to be stopped: reconnaissance was prevented only 10% of the time, credential access from memory around 22%, and one registry-based credential theft variant in less than 1% of attempts.

The article highlights Mimikatz results to show the gap between signature-based detection and behavior-based defense. Dumping credentials from LSASS process memory was blocked almost every time, while pulling credentials from other memory locations or the registry was almost never blocked. Logging improved, but alerts remained at 14%, meaning fewer than one in seven simulated attacks produced an alert, so the article argues organizations must validate exploitable exposure, harden against quiet internal actions, and treat detection rules as an engineering problem.

  • The report suggests that many controls are better at recognizing well-known attack patterns than stopping the underlying behavior, as shown by Mimikatz being blocked on the classic LSASS path but rarely blocked when pursuing the same credential-theft goal through quieter routes.
  • The largest defensive gap is not a lack of collected data, because logging reached 58%, but the failure to turn that telemetry into alerts, with the alert score remaining at only 14%.
  • Strong defensive performance appears temporary without continuous validation, since last year’s stronger sectors slipped while prior laggards improved after retesting and fixing exposed control drift.
  • Overall prevention gains can hide worsening coverage against specific high-risk threats, as prevention fell against nine of the ten hardest-to-stop threat groups and all top ransomware families were blocked less than 38% of the time.
  • Quiet attacker preparation steps such as domain mapping, share and session enumeration, and passive credential access need the same testing focus as louder actions like lateral movement, because attackers can use them to prepare before triggering noisier controls.

The article explains findings from Picus Labs’ Blue Report 2026, which tested real company computer systems and found that defenses are getting better at stopping attacks at the outside edge but are much weaker once an attacker is already inside. Companies and organizations using these defenses are affected because attackers can often quietly look around, find shared resources, and collect passwords or other access information without being stopped. This matters because those quiet early steps can prepare the way for more serious break-ins, while many organizations are recording activity but not turning it into warnings people can act on.

Lazarus Exploits Windows Zero-Day to Gain SYSTEM Access and Deploy Backdoor

Lazarus Group exploited a newly patched Windows zero-day to gain SYSTEM privileges and deploy backdoors against defense and aerospace targets in multiple countries. The campaign used fake job offers, trojanized PDF tools, and compromised legitimate infrastructure to make the attacks appear trustworthy and evade detection.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Check Point Research attributed a Lazarus Group campaign to the zero-day exploitation of CVE-2026-68820, a Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock privilege escalation flaw patched by Microsoft in August 2026.
  • 02The campaign is part of Operation Dream Job and targets defense and aerospace companies in France, Germany, Brazil, and India using fake recruiter messages and job offers.
  • 03One infection chain uses DLL side-loading with a malicious libmupdf.dll to run MISTPEN, which retrieves modules through Microsoft Graph API and OneDrive before deploying ForestTiger.
  • 04A second infection chain uses a trojanized SecurityPDF viewer that decrypts and launches an embedded payload when a specially marked PDF is opened, loading the Troy backdoor into memory.
  • 05The attackers used compromised WordPress, SharePoint, and vulnerable Roundcube servers as ForestTiger command-and-control infrastructure, and some Roundcube servers were infected with the RelayShell PHP web shell.

The Lazarus Group has been attributed by Check Point Research to the zero-day exploitation of CVE-2026-68820, a Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock privilege escalation flaw patched by Microsoft in August 2026. The campaign targeted defense and aerospace companies in France, Germany, Brazil, and India. The activity is part of Operation Dream Job, a long-running campaign that uses fake recruiter messages and job offers to trick professionals into opening malicious files or installing malware.

The attacks used two parallel infection sequences. One used DLL side-loading with a malicious libmupdf.dll to display a bogus job description while stealthily downloading and executing MISTPEN, which communicated through Microsoft Graph API and OneDrive before triggering the AFD.sys exploit and deploying ForestTiger. The other used a trojanized SecurityPDF viewer impersonating Enveil software, which launched the Troy backdoor when a specially marked PDF was opened.

After exploiting the Windows flaw, the attackers obtained SYSTEM privileges and injected another instance of MISTPEN into a SYSTEM process. The campaign also used an updated FudModule 3.1 rootkit that could tamper with Windows Smart App Control, along with compromised WordPress, SharePoint, and vulnerable Roundcube servers as command-and-control infrastructure. Check Point said the campaign was dangerous because Lazarus combined the zero-day with trusted-looking websites, real vendor branding, search-visible fake portals, and compromised legitimate infrastructure.

  • The campaign shows that checking whether a site or download appears legitimate is not enough, because Lazarus used real vendor branding, search-visible fake sites, and compromised legitimate infrastructure to make the infection chain look trustworthy.
  • The attackers reduced the effectiveness of reputation-based defenses by using already compromised WordPress, SharePoint, and Roundcube servers instead of relying only on newly created attacker infrastructure.
  • The trojanized SecurityPDF viewer only activated its embedded payload when opening a PDF with a specific marker, which could help the malware avoid revealing malicious behavior during ordinary use or basic inspection.
  • The updated FudModule 3.1 rootkit specifically tampered with Windows Smart App Control after gaining SYSTEM privileges, showing that the campaign targeted built-in Windows trust and application-safety mechanisms as part of evasion.
  • At least one breached France-based organization was used to send phishing messages to new victims, highlighting that trusted senders can become part of the attack chain once compromised.

A North Korean hacking group called Lazarus used fake recruiter messages and job offers to trick people at defense and aerospace companies in France, Germany, Brazil, and India into opening harmful files or installing a fake PDF reader. The attack took advantage of a newly fixed Windows flaw to give the hackers full control of infected computers and install hidden access tools. It matters because the attackers copied real company branding, used trusted-looking websites, and even abused already-compromised organizations, making the scam much harder for ordinary people to recognize.

OpenAI, Anthropic, Google API Flaw Let Weaker AI Models Decode Stronger Models' Reasoning

Researchers found that encrypted reasoning blocks in OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google APIs could be replayed across sessions and decoded by compatible weaker models, exposing hidden reasoning and secrets from published agent logs. The providers reportedly mitigated the demonstrated attacks, but developers should strip opaque reasoning fields before sharing or committing API traces.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Researchers disclosed a flaw in how OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google carried hidden AI reasoning between API calls, allowing internal reasoning and secrets from session logs to be recovered without cracking the encryption.
  • 02The attack required obtaining an encrypted reasoning block, such as one published in an agent log, and API access to a compatible model from the same provider, rather than providing arbitrary access to private chats.
  • 03Across 6,708 public agent trajectories, the researchers decoded 315,320 thinking blocks and counted 704 distinct privacy artifacts from genuine user sessions after excluding benchmark sources.
  • 04The recovered artifacts included 62 API keys, 33 passwords, 24 access tokens, and seven private keys, with 64 artifacts appearing only in hidden reasoning and not in the visible trace.
  • 05The researchers disclosed the findings to affected providers and others, and said the demonstrated attacks stopped working after mitigations, with the main extraction attack no longer reproducible as of August 2026.

Researchers disclosed a flaw in how OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google carried hidden AI reasoning between API calls. The weakness affected encrypted reasoning objects used by reasoning APIs, where a block created in one session could be replayed into another and, in testing, handed to a weaker model in the same provider family to reveal hidden content. The encryption itself was not cracked, and the attack relied on intact opaque blocks being accepted and processed by the provider.

The team behind the paper “Stealing Reasoning Traces from Proprietary LLM APIs” demonstrated abuse paths including stealing proprietary reasoning for model distillation, extracting private data from published traces, recovering harmful content concealed behind safe visible answers, and hiding prompt injections inside opaque reasoning blocks. Across 6,708 public agent trajectories, the team decoded 315,320 thinking blocks and counted 704 distinct privacy artifacts from genuine user sessions after excluding benchmark sources. These included 62 API keys, 33 passwords, 24 access tokens, and seven private keys.

The cross-user attack required obtaining an encrypted reasoning block, such as one published in an agent log, and API access to a compatible model from the same provider; it did not provide arbitrary access to private chats. The researchers disclosed the findings to affected model providers, Microsoft, and Hugging Face, and said the demonstrated attacks stopped working after mitigations, with the main extraction attack no longer reproducible as of August 2026. The article advises developers to strip reasoning blocks and opaque reasoning fields from shared traces and avoid committing raw API transcripts even when visible text has been sanitized.

  • Sanitizing only the visible text of shared API transcripts was insufficient, because 64 recovered secrets appeared only inside hidden reasoning blocks and nowhere in the readable conversation.
  • The weakness was not a cryptographic break; it came from providers accepting intact opaque reasoning objects across sessions, users, and models.
  • Published agent logs were the central real-world exposure point, meaning the risk was concentrated among developers who shared raw traces with reasoning objects still attached rather than all API users equally.
  • The same portability that enabled secret recovery also allowed an invisible prompt-injection proof of concept, where a malicious instruction was hidden in an opaque reasoning block and later affected an unrelated task.
  • The public record leaves unresolved whether already-published reasoning blocks remain decodable, even though the researchers say fresh versions of the demonstrated attacks no longer work.

Researchers found that hidden “thinking” data used by OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google systems could be copied from one session into another and made visible, sometimes revealing secrets like API keys and passwords from public agent logs. This did not let attackers read anyone’s private chats, but it affected developers who published raw logs with those hidden blocks still inside. The companies were told about the issue, and the researchers say the tested attacks no longer work, but the finding matters because information that looked safely hidden could still expose private data if shared.

Two Brands in One Message, One URL Built at Runtime

A phishing email disguised as a DocuSign remittance notice used a clean-scanning HTML attachment to impersonate Microsoft SharePoint and build its credential-harvesting redirect only after the victim submitted a form. The key lesson is that messages with no visible links and benign file verdicts can still hide phishing logic that runs client-side after user interaction.
KEY POINTS
  • 01A shared remittance mailbox at a medical device manufacturer received an unauthenticated email styled as a DocuSign notice about a completed payment document.
  • 02The email’s visible call-to-action pointed to an empty anchor, while the real lure was a 16,462-byte HTML attachment that the file scanner marked clean.
  • 03Opening the attachment displayed a fake Microsoft SharePoint secure access page with a locked document label and a form asking the recipient to enter a work address.
  • 04The attachment’s inline script built the destination URL only after form submission, using Google redirect endpoints and a base64-encoded recipient address in the fragment.
  • 05Adaptive AI labeled the message as invoice phishing with 90 confidence, and the incident record said it was automatically resolved as phishing.

A shared remittance mailbox at a medical device manufacturer received an unauthenticated message styled as a DocuSign notice about a completed payment document. The sending path did not support the claimed legitimacy: SPF failed, DKIM was absent, DMARC recorded no policy or action, the Return-Path was empty, and the Message-ID ended at localhost. The visible call to action in the email pointed to an empty anchor, while the real lure was a 16,462-byte HTML attachment that the scanner marked clean.

Opening the attachment showed a different impersonation: a fake Microsoft SharePoint secure access page asking the recipient to enter a work address to unlock a locked PDF labeled CheckRemit-requestedDocuments.pdf. The attachment contained no normal hyperlink to the phishing destination; instead, inline script built the destination only after the form was submitted, then redirected the browser after fake verification messages. The reconstructed chain wrapped Google redirect endpoints around an encoded decoy ad-tracker-like value and ended with a fragment parameter carrying a base64-encoded version of the recipient address, though the article states the chain was not navigated and its functionality was not confirmed.

  • A clean attachment verdict was misleading in this case because the file contained markup, styling, and script rather than macros, an executable, or an exploit attempt.

A shared payment mailbox at a medical device manufacturer received a fake DocuSign payment message, but the real trick was a small web-page attachment that pretended to be Microsoft SharePoint and asked the reader to enter a work email address. The message had no working link in the email itself, and the attachment was marked clean, because the dangerous web address was only created after someone filled in the form. This matters because ordinary-looking payment emails can be used to steal work sign-in details, especially in remittance and business payment situations where large losses are common.

CVE-2026-10579 is a critical pre-authentication authentication bypass in Red Hat JBoss EAP’s PicketLink SAML federation that could let attackers forge identities, including admin roles, via exposed SAML response endpoints. KEY POINTS
  • 01CVE-2026-10579 is a critical authentication bypass in PicketLink Federation, the SAML identity federation component shipped with Red Hat JBoss Enterprise Application Platform.
  • 02The flaw allows a pre-authentication attacker with network access to the SAML response endpoint to submit forged assertions naming any principal and role, including administrator accounts.
