CVE-2026-10579 is a critical authentication bypass in PicketLink Federation, the SAML identity federation component shipped with Red Hat JBoss Enterprise Application Platform. Red Hat published the record on August 11, 2026 and rated the security impact as Critical, with a CVSS v3.1 base score of 9.8. The vulnerability affects Red Hat JBoss Enterprise Application Platform 7 and 8, but specific vulnerable or fixed version ranges had not been named at the time of writing.

The flaw is in the handler that processes unsolicited SAML responses, which accepts forged assertions without verification or validation. Exploitation is pre-authentication and requires only network access to the endpoint that consumes SAML responses, with no credentials, user interaction, or prior foothold required. An attacker can construct a SAML assertion naming any principal and role, including administrator accounts, and the application behind the federation layer receives a session that appears authenticated and authorized.

The article says exposed assets are Java application servers acting as SAML service providers where PicketLink federation is configured and the SAML response endpoint is reachable from an untrusted network. No fixed version had been published at the time of writing, so every JBoss EAP instance with PicketLink federation configured should be treated as vulnerable until Red Hat states otherwise. Recommended actions include inventorying JBoss EAP instances, restricting access to SAML service provider endpoints, disabling unsolicited response handling where it is not required, monitoring authentication logs, auditing recent privileged sessions, and rotating SAML signing certificates and session secrets on instances showing anomalous assertions.

  • Scoping exposure by JBoss EAP version alone is insufficient because the advisory does not provide fixed or vulnerable version ranges and the relevant risk depends on whether the deployed picketlink-federation component is configured.
  • The article frames the exposure as an inventory gap because organizations may know their JBoss EAP versions but not whether PicketLink federation is enabled or which endpoints accept unsolicited responses.
  • SAML service provider endpoints are often intentionally reachable from broad external sources because federated login must support users coming from different locations, which makes access restriction operationally harder.
  • Consumer Discretionary, Financials, and Information Technology account for most observed exposed assets in the article’s dataset, with Consumer Discretionary leading at 32.7%.
  • Disabling unsolicited response handling is a targeted mitigation for deployments that do not require identity-provider-initiated login, rather than a broad shutdown of SAML federation.

The article describes a critical flaw in Red Hat JBoss Enterprise Application Platform that can let someone get into affected applications by pretending to be any user, even an administrator, without needing a password. It affects JBoss EAP 7 and 8 systems that use PicketLink Federation for single sign-on and have the login response endpoint reachable from an untrusted network. This matters because these systems often protect business, partner, and customer account applications, and no fixed version had been released when the article was written.

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-72766) n8n Arbitrary File Read and SSRF via Send Email Node

CVE-2026-72766 is a high-severity n8n Send Email node flaw that can let attackers read local files or perform SSRF when exposed unauthenticated webhooks pass untrusted input into email body fields. Organizations should upgrade to fixed n8n versions and audit externally reachable instances and workflows.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CVE-2026-72766 is a type confusion vulnerability in the n8n Send Email node that can cause Nodemailer to interpret non-string workflow expression values as a file path or URL instead of message text.
  • 02Exploitation requires an active unauthenticated webhook, valid SMTP credentials configured on the Send Email node, and untrusted input mapped directly into the text or html body field.
  • 03If exploited, the vulnerability can disclose local files on the n8n host and enable server-side request forgery from inside the network segment where n8n runs.
  • 04The vulnerability affects n8n versions before 1.123.67, 2.x versions before 2.31.5, and 2.32.x versions before 2.32.1.
  • 05n8n patched the issue in versions 1.123.67, 2.31.5, and 2.32.1, and defenders are advised to inventory externally reachable n8n instances, audit workflows, restrict public webhook access, monitor outbound connections, and rotate SMTP credentials where needed.

CVE-2026-72766 is a high-severity type confusion vulnerability in the Send Email node of n8n, an open-source workflow automation platform. The node does not enforce that message fields contain string values, allowing a non-string value from a workflow expression to reach Nodemailer. Nodemailer can then interpret the value as a file path or URL rather than message text. The issue has a CVSS v3.1 score of 7.5 and a CVSS v4.0 score of 8.2.

Exploitation does not require authentication to the n8n instance itself, but the article states that three configuration conditions must already exist. An active workflow must expose an unauthenticated webhook, valid SMTP credentials must be configured on the Send Email node, and untrusted input must be mapped directly into the text or html body field. Where those conditions are met, an attacker who can reach the webhook can cause disclosure of local files on the n8n host and server-side request forgery from inside the network segment where n8n runs. The article notes that n8n instances often hold configuration files, environment variables, and stored credentials for systems they automate.

The vulnerability affects n8n versions before 1.123.67, 2.x versions before 2.31.5, and 2.32.x versions before 2.32.1. Patches are available in versions 1.123.67, 2.31.5, and 2.32.1, and organizations are advised to upgrade to the fixed release matching their current branch. The article also recommends inventorying externally reachable n8n instances, auditing workflows for Send Email nodes fed by webhook data, restricting public webhook access, limiting workflow creation and editing permissions, monitoring outbound connections, and rotating SMTP credentials on externally reachable instances.

  • The article emphasizes that the highest-risk n8n instances are often created for experiments, proofs of concept, or departmental workflows because they are more likely to expose unauthenticated webhooks and less likely to be patched.
  • The practical impact of the file-read issue is amplified because n8n commonly stores configuration files, environment variables, and credentials for the many systems it automates.
  • The exposure pattern is described as a visibility and ownership problem rather than an industry-specific problem, with affected-looking assets appearing under subsidiary domains, single-project cloud accounts, and inconsistent hostnames.
  • The article notes that recently published CVE coverage may vary across vulnerability databases, so defenders should verify n8n versions directly against the vendor advisory instead of relying only on scanner results.
  • Remediation requires matching the correct fixed release line, because organizations running n8n 2.31.x are advised to move to 2.31.5 rather than simply jumping to a 2.32.x release.

The article describes a flaw in n8n, a tool used to automate work between different systems, where a poorly configured email step can treat outside input as a file path or web address instead of normal message text. Self-hosted n8n sites on older versions are affected when they have a public webhook, working email credentials, and untrusted input placed directly into the email body. In those cases, someone could make the n8n server reveal local files or contact internal network locations, which matters because these systems often store settings, environment details, and credentials for other tools they automate. Fixes are available, and the article says organizations should update and find exposed n8n instances, especially ones created outside central oversight.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a specific high-severity vulnerability advisory for n8n with available patches and clear real-world impact, including possible local file disclosure and internal network requests from exposed instances. It is broadly relevant to security teams with self-hosted automation tooling, though the article does not report active exploitation and exploitation depends on a non-default workflow configuration.

Control Which Package Registries Your CI Jobs and Developer Machines Use

StepSecurity argues that organizations moving package downloads behind internal registries need visibility across both CI jobs and developer machines, because either can still silently fall back to public registries. Its registry controls show where installs are actually resolving from so teams can enforce private registry use and reduce exposure to compromised packages.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Engineering organizations are moving package downloads away from public registries and behind internal registries so that policies such as cooldown periods and compromised package blocking can apply before packages are installed.
  • 02The article cites malicious versions of axios on npm, two litellm releases on PyPI with a credential stealer, and a republished @bitwarden/cli that stole credentials from a developer machine and used GitHub tokens to inject malicious workflows into CI.
  • 03StepSecurity says internal registries cannot show jobs or developer machines that bypass them, because they only log requests that reached the internal registry.
  • 04The “Jobs should use a secure registry instead of public package registries” control uses Harden Runner to monitor actual outbound network calls from CI jobs and fails when a job calls public registries such as registry.npmjs.org, pypi.org, or registry-1.docker.io.
  • 05The “Developer machines should use a secure registry instead of public package registries” control uses Dev Machine Guard to read package manager configuration files and report each device-and-tool pair’s effective registry and the source of that setting.

The article says many engineering organizations are moving package downloads away from public registries and behind internal registries such as JFrog Artifactory, Sonatype Nexus, Cloudsmith, Google Artifact Registry, or StepSecurity Secure Registry. The goal is to apply policies such as cooldown periods and compromised package blocking before a package is installed. It cites malicious versions of axios on npm, two litellm releases on PyPI carrying a credential stealer, and a republished @bitwarden/cli that stole credentials from a developer machine and used GitHub tokens to inject malicious workflows into CI.

The article argues that declaring a migration to an internal registry is easier than proving it, because jobs and developer machines may still call public registries directly. An internal registry only logs requests that reach it and cannot show installs that bypass it. StepSecurity describes two Overview dashboard controls that close this visibility gap: one for CI jobs and one for developer machines.

The CI control uses Harden Runner to monitor actual outbound network calls during job runs and fails if the job calls public package registries such as registry.npmjs.org, pypi.org, or registry-1.docker.io. The developer machine control uses Dev Machine Guard to read package manager configuration files such as .npmrc and pip.conf, reporting the effective registry and where that value came from for each device and tool pair. The article says enforcement then involves blocking public registries at the network level in CI, centrally setting package manager configuration on developer machines, and applying download-time policies at the registry itself.

  • A CI job can still fail the registry control even when egress blocking prevents the connection, because the baseline records attempted calls to public registries as evidence that something in the job is still trying to bypass the intended registry path.
  • Developer machine compliance has to be checked per package manager, not just per laptop, because the article notes that npm, pnpm, bun, and pip each resolve their own registry settings and can be compliant or noncompliant independently on the same device.
  • The source of a registry setting is important for remediation, because “npm built-in default,” “user config,” and an explicitly configured public registry each point to a different kind of fix.
  • A correctly configured machine-level registry setting may not be enough, because the article says the Package Configs view can catch cases where a project-level file overrides the global configuration.
  • Attribution can connect registry activity back to a specific developer machine or pipeline by appending a device identifier to the Secure Registry API key, so teams can identify who pulled a package later confirmed as compromised.

The article explains that companies are trying to make their work computers and automated build systems download software packages through a private checkpoint instead of directly from public websites. This matters because attackers have recently put harmful versions of well-known packages like axios, litellm, and @bitwarden/cli on public package sites, where they could steal credentials or help tamper with company workflows. Developers and CI jobs are affected because either one may still be reaching public registries without the company realizing it, leaving a gap that the internal registry cannot see.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is primarily a vendor/product-focused best-practice article about gaining visibility into whether CI jobs and developer machines use internal package registries. Although it references real package compromise examples, it does not report a new incident, vulnerability, or urgent advisory, so it is low priority for security professionals to read.

Courier fraud in the UK exceeded £21 million in losses in 2025, with criminals increasingly targeting over-70s through phone or messaging scams that lead victims to hand over bank cards, cash, gold, or jewellery to couriers. The key shift is that fraud groups are blending digital social engineering with physical pickups and luxury-goods laundering to evade traditional banking fraud controls.
KEY POINTS
  • 01City of London Police data published in June 2026 reported that UK courier fraud losses exceeded £21 million in 2025, with individuals over 70 heavily targeted and the highest concentration of offenses in London and the Home Counties.

  • 03UK law enforcement highlighted a 2025 shift toward manipulating victims into visiting multiple jewellers over time to buy gold and expensive jewellery for handover to fraud couriers.

New data published by the City of London Police in June 2026 shows that UK courier fraud losses exceeded £21 million in 2025, with people aged over 70 heavily targeted. The highest concentration of offenses was recorded in London and the Home Counties. The article describes courier fraud as a hybrid cyber-physical social engineering campaign that begins through deceptive contact by phone, email, or messaging platforms and ends with a physical courier collecting assets from the victim.

Fraud syndicates are evolving their tactics by using platforms such as WhatsApp and remotely paying third-party courier services to carry out residential collections. UK law enforcement also highlighted a shift toward high-value physical goods, where victims are manipulated into visiting multiple jewellers over time to buy gold or expensive jewellery and then hand it to fraud couriers. The article says this approach can bypass normal banking security controls because victims are persuaded to withdraw cash, disclose PINs, or make in-person purchases themselves.

Recent UK Regional Organised Crime Unit activity shows the nationwide scale of these networks. In July 2026, North West ROCU arrested two men in Huddersfield and Manchester on suspicion of Conspiracy to Defraud and Money Laundering after suspects allegedly impersonated bank fraud departments, collected a victim’s card, and used it for fraudulent transactions. In June 2026, a North East ROCU case ended with a prison sentence for a primary operative in a network that targeted 14 victims, obtained bank cards and PINs, scammed £56,000, and laundered funds through purchases of smartphones, designer clothing, and luxury jewellery.

  • The shift toward gold and luxury jewellery is described as an evasion tactic because banks may flag unusual transfers, but they cannot easily stop victims from making physical withdrawals or card purchases across multiple retail locations.
  • Fraud groups reduce their own exposure by using unwitting third-party courier services booked remotely, turning ordinary logistics providers into part of the collection process.
  • Courier fraud is difficult to prevent because victims are persuaded to bypass normal banking protections themselves by withdrawing cash, disclosing PINs, or buying high-value goods.
  • The article identifies unusual consecutive high-value purchases by elderly customers at jewellery or luxury retailers as a potentially actionable warning pattern for financial institutions.

The article explains that courier fraud in the UK caused more than £21 million in losses in 2025, with people over 70 heavily targeted, especially in London and the Home Counties. Criminals pretend to be from banks or police, contact victims by phone or messaging apps like WhatsApp, and convince them to hand over bank cards, cash, PINs, gold, or jewellery to couriers. This matters because the scams combine remote deception with someone physically collecting valuables, making it harder for banks and police to stop before victims lose large amounts of money.
